html:
The map's label for the farming peoples of the savanna and Sahel belt south of the Sahara, from the Atlantic to the Horn of Africa, shown from 1500 BCE to 1500. They lived by growing grain crops that were first tamed in Africa itself.

Their main crops:

  • sorghum, tamed in the eastern Sahel;
  • pearl millet, tamed in the western Sahel and grown in the driest places;
  • African rice, bred in the inland delta of the Niger;
  • fonio, cowpeas and groundnuts of local kinds, with cattle, sheep and goats.

These crops travelled far: sorghum and millet reached India around 2000 BCE, the millets from Africa on the India chart.

As the Sahara dried after about 3000 BCE, people moved south into the savanna. Stone villages at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania show farming and herding communities by 2000 BCE. Iron working spread in the first millennium BCE, and the Nok culture of central Nigeria made its famous clay heads. Towns followed: Djenné-Djenno on the Niger was a busy town by 250 BCE.

The farmers' surplus fed the states that later grew rich on the trans-Saharan trade, from Ghana to Mali and Kanem. Most people in these states remained village farmers of the same grains, and still are.
